The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) received patient samples with identifiers removed, but it was not specified whether the assays were performed in a blinded manner to the results. 2. Most studies demonstrated a low potential for reference test bias, except for three studies where the risk was unclear. 3. All studies showed a low potential for flow and timing bias, except for one study by Castro et al., which did not provide a clear description of patient flow. 4. The sensitivity and specificity of the tests were reported as 7%, with some overlap in confidence intervals. 5. The prevalence of syphilis was assessed at 5%, 10%, and 20%, with outcomes reported for true positives, false negatives, true negatives, and false positives across 13 studies involving 3,699 clients. These studies were cross-sectional cohort-type accuracy studies. 6. The certainty of evidence for test accuracy was rated as moderate, with true positives ranging from 45 to 180 per 1,000 clients tested, depending on pre-test probability. False negatives ranged from 5 to 20 per 1,000 clients tested. 7. True negatives were reported in 13 studies involving 6,619 clients, with false positives ranging from 21 to 25 per 1,000 clients tested. The certainty of evidence for these findings was also rated as moderate. 8. Two additional studies were conducted for the non-treponemal component of syphilis testing, as detailed in Web Annex D. 9. Most studies had a low risk of patient selection bias, as assessed using the QUADAS checklist. However, four studies had unclear descriptions of random sampling, and four studies had a high risk of bias due to non-random sampling or oversampling of high-risk individuals. 10. Most studies demonstrated a low potential for index test bias, except for three studies where the risk was unclear. In one study, patient identifiers were removed before receipt at the CDC, but it was not specified if the assay was blinded. Pham et al. reported a high risk of bias. 11. Four studies had an unclear risk of bias for the reference standard. 12. All studies showed a low potential for flow and timing bias, except for two studies that did not provide a clear description of patient flow. 13. The sensitivity and specificity of the tests were reported as 3%, with some overlap in confidence intervals. 14. Evidence profiles for the clinical utility of dual treponemal/non-treponemal rapid diagnostic tests (T/NT RDTs) indicated moderate certainty for their ability to diagnose active syphilis in at-risk populations. 15. Observational studies demonstrated that RDTs were generally acceptable to both patients and healthcare workers. In the Solomon Islands, 1 in 20 healthcare workers reported difficulty drawing blood, but RDTs were considered reliable and easy to use. 16. In Botswana, visual reading of RDTs missed three out of five active syphilis infections, suggesting that digital readers may be advantageous in certain settings. 17. RDTs were associated with a high proportion of appropriately treated active syphilis cases, ranging from 76% to 95%, depending on the reference standard used. 18. The use of RDTs was associated with a significant reduction in overtreatment, ranging from 50% to 100%, depending on the study location. 19. RDT kits were pre-packaged, did not require skilled laboratory technicians, and were not affected by reagent procurement issues, making them particularly suitable for resource-limited settings. 20. The smartphone-based triplex test and the DPP-RDT were viewed favorably by healthcare workers in Rwanda due to their usability in field settings and during power outages. 21. The time to treatment and uptake of testing were not reported in the studies reviewed. 22. Social harms associated with syphilis testing and treatment were not reported in the studies reviewed. 23. The certainty of evidence for the ability of dual T/NT RDTs to reduce overtreatment and appropriately diagnose active syphilis was rated as moderate.
